title: The Pale Room
premise: Ansel Montrose returns to the family estate to bury his twin brother Aurel, only to realize at the funeral that the body in the casket is wearing Ansel's face—and that no one else can tell them apart. The excavation crew hired to repair the flooded cellar unearths a door sealed from the inside, behind which lies a room where their grandmother once taught her children a lullaby whose final verse was never written down. As the house begins singing it back to him, Ansel discovers the truth: whoever completes the verse becomes the house's keeper, and Aurel didn't die—he took Ansel's place and is still inside, alive in the pale room. In the end, Ansel must choose between finishing the song to free his brother (and losing himself) or burning the verse unfinished, sealing Aurel away forever; he sings three lines and stops, leaving both brothers half-kept, as the house settles into an uneasy silence that may not last.
about_author: Cyrus Delacroix is the pen name of a former funeral home archivist who spent seven years cataloguing unclaimed effects before turning to fiction. They write exclusively at night, in rooms with more than one door.

chapters.title: The Wrong Face
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. At Aurel's funeral, Ansel lifts the coffin lid for a private goodbye and finds his own face staring back. The undertaker insists nothing is amiss; the parish records list the deceased as 'A. Montrose.' Ansel's grief curdles into dread. Emotional beat: the uncanny rupture—mourning collapses into the terror of having been replaced.

chapters.title: Doors Counted
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. He moves back into Montrose House, compulsively counting doors each night—eleven, always eleven, though the blueprints show ten. He finds Aurel's journal, its last entry reading only: 'She never finished teaching us.' Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into obsession as the house's geometry refuses to stay honest.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: POV Mara Okafor, foreman of the drainage crew hired to fix the flooded cellar. Her team breaks through a wall and finds a door with its hinges on the inside, bolted shut from within, warm to the touch. Ansel forbids them to open it. Emotional beat: professional skepticism beginning to crack against something older than skepticism.

chapters.title: What the Crew Heard
chapters.summary: POV Mara. Overnight, two workers quit after hearing humming through the door—a lullaby they somehow already knew. Mara stays out of stubbornness and mounting fascination, sketching the door's carvings: verses of a song, the last line chiseled blank. Emotional beat: curiosity as contagion; loyalty to her crew vs. hunger for truth.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Verse
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. Searching the attic, he finds recordings of his grandmother teaching the lullaby to young twins—herself cutting off before the final verse, voice shaking. On tape, a child's voice asks what happens if you sing it whole. Grandmother answers: 'Then the house keeps you.' Emotional beat: inherited guilt; love entangled with duty.

chapters.title: Knocking From Inside
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The knocking starts—rhythmic, patient, matching the lullaby's meter. One worker, Dez, begins sleepwalking toward the cellar, humming harmonies he shouldn't know. Mara realizes the song is learning them even as they learn it. Emotional beat: dread of complicity; survival means refusing to sing along.

chapters.title: Aurel
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. Through the bolted door, a voice—his brother's—speaks his name. Aurel explains: he answered the house's call years ago, wore Ansel's shape outside while his true self was kept in the pale room. He begs Ansel to finish the verse and trade places. Emotional beat: devastating tenderness; love against duty made literal.

chapters.title: The Counting Breaks
chapters.summary: POV Mara. The house adds a twelfth door overnight; Dez walks through it and doesn't return. Mara confronts Ansel with everything—the tapes, the carvings, the missing man—and demands they burn the house down together. Ansel refuses: Aurel is still inside. Emotional beat: alliance fracturing between mercy and mercy's opposite.

chapters.title: Three Lines
chapters.summary: POV Ansel. At the threshold, Ansel sings the first three lines of the final verse. The door unbolts; the pale room opens onto a white corridor where Aurel waits, translucent, smiling. But the fourth line rises in Ansel's own throat, eager, and he understands the trap: the song wants to be finished by someone who wants to finish it. Emotional beat: climax—willpower against longing.

chapters.title: Half-Kept
chapters.summary: POV Ansel and Mara, alternating. Ansel stops mid-line; the house screams through every door at once. He and Mara seal the room with salt, fire, and the unfinished verse itself, written on the door. Aurel's last words: 'Better half than hollow.' Weeks later, the house is quiet—but some nights, faintly, someone hums the first three lines. Emotional beat: bittersweet resolution; survival purchased at the price of wholeness.
